Book Reviews Political Order in Changing Societies, by Samuel P. Huntington. New Haven: Yale University Press, 1968. Pp. xii, 488. $12.50. For years, much has been said about the beneficial impact of the study of new nations on the more traditional domain of American political science. Samuel Huntington's new book, concerned with Asia, Latin America, and to a lesser extent with Africa, reverses the process by restoring a concern with government to its rightful central place in the study of Third World politics. Unlike most scholars in comparative politics, the author does not mince his words. The book opens with a major thrust, already known to many in its previous incarnation as an essay in World Politics: On balance, the most salient phenomenon in the contemporary world is not political develop- ment but political decay. Much as there is a growing economic gap between rich and poor nations, there is a growing gap between nations that have governments and those that don't. The book closes with the proposition that the key to this fundamental difference is the presence or absence of organized politics, especially in the form of political parties. In what is probably the pithiest conclusion to any major work of political science in recent years, Huntington asserts that " in the modernizing world he controls the future who organizes its politics." Between the beginning and the conclusion, Huntington takes us through a series of essays which explore various aspects of the central theme. About one-third of the book restates in expanded form some of the author's previously published ideas. The discussion of " political Development and Political Decay " now specifies more precisely the multi-dimensional character of political modernization and presents more formally a central hypothesis concerning the consequences of a series of successive gaps between social mobilization and economic development, resulting in social frustration; between the latter and mobility opportunities, resulting in political participation; and finally between the latter and political institutionalization, resulting in " prae- torian " politics. The contrast between " praetorianism " and " civic " politics (distinct from the Almond and Verba variety since it includes Communist dictatorships) is ingeniously related to the Aristotelian distinction between " right " and " wrong," or corrupt, constitutions. The second essay, equally provocative, analyses the early developers and exposes, hopefully once and for all, the fallacy of the " America- as-first-nation-and-summit-of-modernization " posture. He discusses the limited potential of traditional monarchies; the somewhat greater capability of military regimes; and ultimately the much greater potential of party govern- ment dedicated to either revolution or reform. Much as does Barring- ton Moore (in a work which is unfortunately not discussed), Hunting- ton views the mobilization of peasants as the key to different outcomes of modernization. It is from the point of view of their relative ability to organize peasants for political participation, indeed, that various types of party government are evaluated in the final chapter. Since I am on record as sharing to a considerable extent Huntington's view that political order is no mere epiphenomenon of modernization but that it must be created, and that this task is the most important initial requirement of political development but also the most difficult to achieve, my assessment that the book's central theme is persuasive carries little critical weight. Undoubtedly, area specialists will object to Huntington's handling of some of the specific case studies which illustrate his various arguments, and others will uncover weaknesses in his handling of cross-national comparisons (such as Table 7.4, p. 423, which does not take into account time segment variations, so that an absence of coup is given equal weight whether a country has been independent for three years or twenty-two). But this is a work which deserves much more extensive discussion than it is possible to provide in an initial review and its quality insures that this it will indeed receive. Meanwhile, two important shortcomings deserve to be pointed out. The first is Hutington's somewhat simple model of societies, which he expects to evolve in a unilinear manner from a traditional state in which differential relations to land are the dominant feature (as in varieties of feudalism) to another state in which class becomes salient. The difficulties this assumption engenders emerge from the discussion of land reform, where Huntington himself is forced to acknowledge- but without explanation-that it does not constitute a salient issue in the politics of Tropical Africa (p. 380). Why not? Clearly because there is a fundamental distinction to be made between peasant and non-peasant societies. But if that is so, one must raise a subsequent question about the applicability of general propositions to moderniza- tion in the world as a whole, as against in specific cultural regions. The other important deficiency is hinted at by one remark about China: Mao, according to Huntington, met his undoing when he abandoned Lenin for Trotsky (p. 343). But is it not possible, alter- natively, that Mao is as creative a political innovator as Lenin was, who has conceptualized anti-organization much as scientists have anti- matter? ARISTIDE R.
